Inbound OT-segment connections from CyberAv3ngers infrastructure (185.82.73.160/28, 135.136.1.133) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts network sessions to or from the Iran-nexus IP infrastructure attributed to the Minnesota water-utility OT campaign. Any connection from 185.82.73.160-171 or 135.136.1.133 toward an internal (especially OT/DMZ) host is high-fidelity intrusion evidence. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker IP block (185.82.73.160-171) and singleton 135.136.1.133 from the article's pre-extracted IOCs; direct IP-match on named threat infrastructure is inherently high-fidelity and near-zero FP for OT environments. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a • https://www.tenable.com/blog/coordinated-cyberattack-on-minnesota-water-utilities-what-you-need-to-know • https://www.tenable.com/blog/what-to-know-about-cyberav3ngers-the-irgc-linked-group-targeting-critical-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1190 T0819
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/scanning platform (Shodan, Censys) sweeping the same block coincidentally reusing a recycled IP
  • Security vendor sinkhole or CTI enrichment traffic hitting the IP for reputation checks
  • Corporate proxy egress where an analyst manually browsed to research the IOC
  • VPN concentrator NAT causing an internal IP to appear as the remote peer
  • Recycled cloud IP later re-leased to a benign SaaS after the campaign window
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_in_range(LocalIP, "185.82.73.160/28"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host/port that talked to the IOC IP; if it is an OT/DMZ asset or engineering workstation, treat as confirmed and pull full session/PCAP. 2) Contain: block 185.82.73.160/28 and 135.136.1.133 at the perimeter and OT boundary firewall, isolate the affected host from the OT segment, and force it to manual/known-good control. 3) Hunt: sweep firewall + EDR for any other internal host touching the block, pivot to CVE-2021-22681/2023-3595/2024-6242 exploitation attempts against MicroLogix/ControlLogix PLCs, and check for PLC config/firmware changes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "185.82.73.160/28") or RemoteIP == "135.136.1.133"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "185.82.73.160/28") or SourceIP == "135.136.1.133"
   or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, "185.82.73.160/28") or DestinationIP == "135.136.1.133"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-sourced access to OT/ICS PLCs on EtherNet/IP, Modbus & S7comm ports AIDelivery Medium
Hunts external (non-RFC1918) connections reaching OT control-protocol ports (EtherNet/IP 44818/2222, Modbus 502, S7comm 102, DNP3 20000, BACnet 47808) — the exposure CISA warns enabled the Minnesota MicroLogix 1400 compromise. Any allowed inbound session from the internet to these ports is the attack surface the actors used. Rationale: Targets the exact exposure CISA flagged (internet-reachable Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix PLCs) using the canonical ICS control-protocol ports EtherNet/IP TCP/44818 & 2222 named in the kill-chain hint; scoping to public source + allowed action keeps it to genuine internet exposure. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because this is perimeter-firewall telemetry, not endpoint or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/rockwell-plcs-removed/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a
ATT&CKT1190 T0883 T0866
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor remote-support session to a PLC over a whitelisted static IP
  • SCADA integrator polling a cloud historian across a site-to-site link that terminates as 'public' at the firewall
  • Managed-service OT monitoring appliance reaching the field device from a hosted IP
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys) probing 44818/502 producing allowed-but-unanswered logs
  • Misclassified NAT where an internal SCADA host appears with a public source address
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic([]))  // populate with approved vendor remote-support source IPs to suppress sanctioned maintenance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the destination is a real PLC/RTU and whether the source is an approved vendor IP; unapproved public source to 44818/502/102 = treat as active reconnaissance/exploitation. 2) Contain: drop the exposure at the OT boundary firewall (deny internet→OT control ports), place the PLC behind a jump host/VPN, and verify controller run-state and program integrity. 3) Hunt: correlate the same source IP against the CyberAv3ngers block, look for CVE-2021-22681/2023-3595/2024-6242 exploit patterns, and inventory every other field device reachable from the internet.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (44818, 2222, 502, 102, 20000, 47808)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where toint(DestinationPort) in (44818, 2222, 502, 102, 20000, 47808)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","allowed","accept","permit","permitted") or isempty(DeviceAction)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix PLCs exposed to campaign CVEs AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces managed assets carrying the three ICS CVEs the actors exploited (CVE-2021-22681 auth bypass, CVE-2023-3595 ControlLogix RCE, CVE-2024-6242) so the SOC can prioritise isolation/patching of the exact attack surface used against the Minnesota utilities. Posture/attack-surface hunt rather than live-event detection. Rationale: Pins to the three named CVEs (CVE-2021-22681 / CVE-2023-3595 / CVE-2024-6242) and Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix devices from the article and kill-chain block; joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact internet-exposed-PLC surface the actors used. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty — this is inventory/TVM data with no single-event log shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a • https://www.tenable.com/blog/what-to-know-about-cyberav3ngers-the-irgc-linked-group-targeting-critical-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1190 T0819
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PLC already air-gapped/segmented so CVE presence is not internet-exploitable (still worth patching but lower priority)
  • TVM version fingerprint stale after a firmware update not yet re-scanned
  • Non-production lab/bench PLC flagged alongside production assets
  • Vendor-managed device where patching is contractually deferred
  • Duplicate DeviceId entries from re-imaged engineering workstations inflating counts
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by IsInternetFacing then by CVE severity; any internet-facing MicroLogix/ControlLogix with CVE-2021-22681 or CVE-2023-3595 is top priority. 2) Contain: remove the controller from direct internet exposure (CISA 'CI Fortify' guidance), place behind VPN/jump host, and schedule the Rockwell firmware update. 3) Hunt: for each vulnerable device, pull firewall logs for inbound 44818/502/102 from the CyberAv3ngers block and verify controller program/firmware has not been altered.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2021-22681", "CVE-2023-3595", "CVE-2024-6242")
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, CveId asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2021-22681", "CVE-2023-3595", "CVE-2024-6242")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by CveId asc
Coordinated fan-out from CyberAv3ngers infrastructure across multiple OT sites AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the coordinated, multi-utility signature of the campaign — a single attacker IP (or the 185.82.73.160/28 block) reaching many distinct internal OT endpoints inside a short window, matching the '30+ community water systems on July 26-27' disruption. Threshold/temporal-correlation alert flagging campaign-scale activity, not a single probe. Rationale: Combines the named attacker block with a fan-out threshold (one source IP → 3+ distinct internal OT endpoints in 1h) to model the article's defining trait: a single coordinated operation hitting 30+ utilities simultaneously — separating campaign-scale impact from an isolated scan. Threshold/temporal correlation, so no Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://www.tenable.com/blog/coordinated-cyberattack-on-minnesota-water-utilities-what-you-need-to-know • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a
ATT&CKT0827 T0828 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate central vendor/MSSP polling multiple sites from one hosted IP (fan-out looks identical)
  • Shared NAT/proxy where many benign flows appear to originate from one address in the block
  • Load-balancer or CDN health-check hitting several internal endpoints
  • Backup/replication service reaching multiple OT DMZ hosts on a schedule
  • Internet scanner sweeping the org's public ranges across several assets
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic([]))  // add sanctioned central-management/MSSP source IPs to suppress benign multi-site polling
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is inside the CyberAv3ngers block and list the distinct internal targets and ports; multi-site OT targeting = declare incident and notify MNIT/CISA-equivalent. 2) Contain: block the block org-wide at all boundaries, isolate every touched OT host, and switch affected plants to manual/known-good operation. 3) Hunt: verify PLC run-state and program/firmware integrity on each target, pull exploit evidence for CVE-2021-22681/2023-3595/2024-6242, and check for loss-of-comms/controller-stop events coinciding with the fan-out window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "185.82.73.160/28") or RemoteIP == "135.136.1.133"
| summarize DistinctHosts = dcount(DeviceName), Hosts = make_set(DeviceName, 50), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctHosts >= 3   // 3+ distinct internal OT hosts hit by one attacker IP in 1h = coordinated fan-out
| order by DistinctHosts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "185.82.73.160/28") or SourceIP == "135.136.1.133"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 50), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctTargets >= 3   // 3+ distinct internal targets from one campaign IP in 1h = coordinated multi-site activity
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (CIDR(@DestinationIp, 185.82.73.160/28) OR @DestinationIp:135.136.1.133)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| cidr("185.82.73.160/28", field=RemoteAddressIP4) OR RemoteAddressIP4="135.136.1.133"
| groupBy([RemoteAddressIP4], function=count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=DistinctHosts))
| DistinctHosts >= 3

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.src IN ("185.82.73.160","185.82.73.161","185.82.73.162","185.82.73.163","185.82.73.164","185.82.73.165","185.82.73.166","185.82.73.167","185.82.73.168","185.82.73.169","185.82.73.170","185.82.73.171","135.136.1.133")) by All_Traffic.src span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(src)` | where distinct_targets >= 3 | sort - distinct_targets

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-22681", "CVE-2023-3595", "CVE-2024-6242")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-22681", "CVE-2023-3595", "CVE-2024-6242")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Endpoint contact with F6 fraud-campaign hosting infra (212.127.73.235 / 167.86.100.68) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts outbound endpoint or perimeter connections to the fixed IP addresses that host the bulk of the F6 advance-payment fraud clone sites. Any internal host resolving/reaching this infrastructure indicates a user was steered to a counterfeit Russian-company site controlled by the fraudsters. Rationale: Uses the two campaign IPs named in the article body (212.127.73.235, 167.86.100.68) that F6 states host 'the vast majority' of the ~100 clone domains, plus two related IPs from the extracted IOC set. Fixed-IP contact is a clean, deployable alert pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-fraud-campaign.html

DNS / web resolution of F6 counterfeit Russian-company domains AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS queries or web connections to the specific counterfeit domains used in the F6 fraud campaign (ruspromexport-group.ru and agrocenter-eurohem.ru, including mail/www hosts). Resolution of these lookalike domains from an internal host indicates a user is interacting with a fraudster-controlled clone of a legitimate Russian supplier. Rationale: Uses the two exact counterfeit domains named in the article (ruspromexport-group.ru and the 2017-era agrocenter-eurohem.ru clone). Domain resolution is unambiguous — these hostnames have no legitimate use, so a hit is a high-fidelity indicator with negligible FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-fraud-campaign.html

Inbound email from F6 fraud clone domain (ruspromexport-group.ru / info@ruspromexport-group.ru) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose sender/envelope domain matches the fraudster-controlled clone infrastructure. F6 documented that operators send commercial offers, contracts and invoices with bogus bank details from fake corporate mailboxes such as info@ruspromexport-group.ru to route advance payments to criminal accounts. Rationale: Uses the fraud mailbox/domain named in the extracted IOC set (info@ruspromexport-group.ru, ruspromexport-group.ru, mail.ruspromexport-group.ru). Sender-domain match on a dedicated fraud clone domain is high-fidelity; the AttachmentCount projection surfaces the bogus contract/invoice PDFs F6 describes. Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine

Researchers Show a Single Malicious Webpage Visit Can Compromise Tor Browser

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Nebula Security says a patched Firefox JIT flaw could be triggered by simply visiting a malicious webpage and was also used to compromise Tor Browser. Tracked as CVE-2026-10702, the bug provides arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process. Mozilla rated it High and fixed it in the Firefox 151.0.3 update. "No settings or additional user interaction are required," Eten Zou,

Vulnerable Firefox exposed to CVE-2026-10702 JIT RCE (147 through 151.0.2) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints running a Firefox build in the vulnerable range for CVE-2026-10702, the ObjectToIterator JIT type-confusion flaw Nebula Security weaponised as IonStack stage 1. Hunts exposure since a single malicious webpage visit yields renderer RCE with no user interaction; patched only in 151.0.3 (ESR 140.12 unaffected). Rationale: Uses the exact CVE (CVE-2026-10702) and its patched build (151.0.3) from the article; a direct TVM CVE match is unambiguous exposure, no version-string parsing needed. Cross-checked against Rapid7 MFSA-2026-54 and Mozilla's advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/db/vulnerabilities/mfsa2026-54-cve-2026-10702/ • https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10702/
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint patched to 151.0.3 but TVM inventory not yet re-scanned (stale snapshot shows old version)
  • Firefox ESR 140.12 mis-catalogued into the vulnerable range by the scanner (article confirms ESR is NOT affected)
  • Portable/second Firefox install TVM cannot version-resolve, reported as generic 'firefox'
  • Developer/nightly channel builds carrying a version string outside the stable range
  • Kiosk or air-gapped hosts that never touch the internet (exposure present but exploit path blocked)
Suppression filter
| where not (SoftwareName has "esr" and SoftwareVersion startswith "140.12")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <=151.0.2 (or ESR <140.12) and the host has browser internet access; discount ESR 140.12 hits. 2) Contain: push Firefox 151.0.3 (or ESR 140.12) via patch management; for high-value hosts, temporarily restrict outbound browsing until updated. 3) Hunt: on any host that browsed before patching, pivot to UC 'Firefox renderer process spawning child' to check for actual renderer RCE, and review proxy logs for the browsing that preceded any anomaly.

Outdated Tor Browser bundling vulnerable Firefox (CVE-2026-10702 exposure) AIExploitation Medium
Tor Browser bundles Firefox and is not catalogued by vulnerability scanners, so TVM misses it. This hunts running Tor Browser firefox.exe instances, parses the bundled Firefox product version, and flags builds in the 147 through 151.0.2 range vulnerable to the IonStack stage-1 JIT RCE. Directly addresses the article's headline that every Tor Browser release carrying a vulnerable Firefox is affected. Rationale: Article headline is Tor-Browser-specific and TVM cannot see Tor's bundled Firefox, so this parses ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion against the exact vulnerable range (147–151.0.2, patched 151.0.3) and scopes to the 'Tor Browser' install path. Version-range logic mirrors the article's stated affected range. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html • https://security.lookout.com/threat-intelligence/article/cve-2026-10702-firefox-for-android-jit-type-confusion-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User already updated Tor Browser but an old cached process execution still sits in the 14-day window
  • Tor Browser Alpha/nightly channel reporting a non-stable version string that mis-parses
  • Portable Tor Browser run from a USB/Downloads path not containing 'Tor Browser' folder name (missed, not FP — coverage gap)
  • Version info field blank on some builds, yielding null Major (row dropped, not FP)
  • Legitimate privacy-conscious users for whom Tor usage itself is sanctioned — exposure is real but not malicious activity
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parsed Version is truly <=151.0.2 and the Tor Browser is actively used (recent LastSeen). 2) Contain: instruct user to update Tor Browser to the release bundling Firefox 151.0.3+, or remove unsanctioned Tor installs per policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the host's Tor usage window against UC 'Firefox renderer spawning child' and any local privilege-escalation signals (GhostLock CVE-2026-43499), since browser patching does not remove the kernel LPE.

| where FolderPath has "Tor Browser" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Tor Browser"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Ver = ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
| extend P = split(Ver, ".")
| extend Major = toint(P[0]), Minor = toint(P[1]), Build = toint(P[2])
| where Major >= 147 and Major <= 151          // vulnerable Firefox range per article
| where not (Major == 151 and Build >= 3)        // 151.0.3 is the patched build
| summarize LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Version=any(Ver), FolderPath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, AccountName, Major, Minor, Build
| order by LastSeen desc

| extend P = split(Ver, ".")
| extend Major = toint(P[0]), Build = toint(P[2])
| where Major >= 147 and Major <= 151
| where not (Major == 151 and Build >= 3)

Firefox/Tor renderer (content) process spawning an unexpected child — sandbox escape / RCE AIExploitation Medium
Detects a Firefox content/renderer process (firefox.exe launched with -contentproc) spawning a non-Firefox child process. Renderer processes are sandboxed and normally spawn nothing; a child indicates code execution inside the renderer — the exact CVE-2026-10702 primitive (arbitrary code execution in the browser's renderer process) and the pivot toward the GhostLock kernel stage. Architecture-independent per Nebula, so relevant on desktop Windows/Linux. Rationale: Grounds on the article's core primitive ('arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process') and Firefox's own multiprocess architecture: the -contentproc flag uniquely marks the sandboxed renderer, and a renderer spawning any non-Firefox child is a high-fidelity sandbox-escape/RCE signal that precedes the GhostLock kernel stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-54/ • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/06/one-malicious-link-full-root-access.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firefox invoking the OS default handler for a downloaded file or a custom URL-scheme protocol (e.g. opening a PDF/mailto) from a content process
  • WebRTC/native-messaging host or browser extension helper legitimately launched from the content process
  • Third-party AV/DLP injecting into and spawning from firefox.exe
  • Crash-handling helpers not in the exclusion list on niche builds
  • Enterprise browser-management agents shelling out from Firefox context
Suppression filter
| where ChildProcess !in~ ("AcroRd32.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe") and ChildPath !has "\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process image, path and command line — LOLBins (cmd, powershell, sh, /tmp payloads) or unsigned binaries from the renderer are near-certain true positives; a signed OS file handler is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Firefox process tree, and capture volatile memory for the renderer PID before reboot. 3) Hunt: check the host for CVE-2026-43499/GhostLock local-privilege-escalation activity (unexpected root/SYSTEM child from the same tree), review proxy logs for the malicious page visited immediately prior, and confirm Firefox/Tor build against the vulnerable-version UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "firefox.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"   // the sandboxed renderer/content child
| where FileName !in~ ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RendererCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildPath = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "firefox.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-contentproc"
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RendererCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\firefox.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '-contentproc'
  filter_helpers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\plugin-container.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\crashreporter.exe'
      - '\pingsender.exe'
      - '\minidump-analyzer.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_helpers
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*-contentproc* -@Image:(*\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\plugin-container.exe OR *\updater.exe OR *\crashreporter.exe OR *\pingsender.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/firefox\.exe$/i
| regex("-contentproc", field=ParentCommandLine)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/(firefox|plugin-container|updater|crashreporter|pingsender|minidump-analyzer)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="firefox.exe" Processes.parent_process="*-contentproc*" NOT Processes.process_name IN ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="firefox.exe" Processes.parent_process="*-contentproc*" NOT Processes.process_name IN ("firefox.exe","plugin-container.exe","updater.exe","crashreporter.exe","pingsender.exe","minidump-analyzer.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Endpoint exposed to GhostLock kernel futex LPE (CVE-2026-43499, IonStack stage 2) AIExploitation Low
Surfaces Linux hosts exposed to CVE-2026-43499 (GhostLock), the kernel futex flaw Nebula uses as IonStack's second stage to carry renderer RCE to root. The article explicitly warns that patching Firefox blocks the browser entry point but does NOT patch GhostLock, so this exposure must be tracked independently of the browser fix. Rationale: Uses the article's second CVE (CVE-2026-43499 / GhostLock) and its explicit operational caveat that the kernel flaw persists after Firefox is patched; TVM CVE match gives clean, independent LPE-exposure tracking for the privilege-escalation phase. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researchers-show-single-malicious.html • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319914/20260708/public-exploit-turns-15-year-linux-kernel-flaw-5-second-root-attack.htm
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host kernel already patched but TVM snapshot stale, still showing the CVE
  • Backported vendor kernel (RHEL/Ubuntu) where the fix is applied but version string still matches the scanner's vulnerable pattern
  • Containers inheriting the host kernel version double-counted as separate assets
  • Embedded/appliance Linux where the futex path is not reachable in practice
  • Non-Android Linux hosts with no browser present (exposure real but full IonStack chain not applicable)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running kernel is genuinely unpatched (uname -r vs vendor fixed build) and not a backport false match. 2) Contain: schedule/expedite kernel patching; for internet-facing or browser-heavy hosts, prioritise since GhostLock is invoked directly from the browser. 3) Hunt: on exposed hosts, review for renderer-escape activity (UC: Firefox renderer spawning child) and any unexpected transition to root/uid 0 from a user-context process, which would indicate GhostLock was actually fired.

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10702", "CVE-2026-43499")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

Check Point mgmt server contact from CVE-2026-16232 exploitation source IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts network contact between any monitored host/appliance and the six source IPs Check Point attributed to in-the-wild CVE-2026-16232 SmartConsole authentication-bypass exploitation. Article-specific because it keys on the exact attacker infrastructure targeting internet-exposed Security Management / MDS servers. Rationale: Uses the six exact source IPs Check Point published for observed CVE-2026-16232 exploitation; corroborated by Check Point CheckMates, Security Affairs and Help Net Security, so they are shipped as multi-source-confirmed IOCs rather than single-article claims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-technical-analysis-cve-2026-16232/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195848/hacking/check-point-patches-actively-exploited-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-flaw.html • https://community.checkpoint.com/t5/Firewall-and-Security-Management/CVE-2026-16232-Active-Exploitation-Requires-Immediate-Management/td-p/280065 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/check-point-vulnerability-cve-2026-16232/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned external vulnerability scanner or pentest that happens to route through a reassigned IP now inside this set
  • IP reassigned by the ISP to a benign tenant after the campaign window
  • Threat-intel validation/sandbox host in your own org resolving these IPs
  • Shared NAT/VPN egress where an unrelated customer previously used the address
  • Firewall log replay/backfill re-ingesting historical events after the fact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal asset is the peer and whether it is the Security Management / MDS server or an admin jump host; pull the surrounding CommonSecurityLog events for that SourceIP and check whether the mgmt interface is internet-exposed with unrestricted Trusted Clients. 2) Contain: block the six IPs at the perimeter, restrict SmartConsole Trusted Clients to approved subnets, and verify the July 22 2026 Jumbo Hotfix (R81.20/R82.10) is applied; if not, treat the mgmt server as potentially compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 for any admin login or policy-install activity from these IPs, and review all administrator accounts and SmartConsole SSO tickets issued in the exposure window.

Check Point SmartConsole admin login via forged application token (CVE-2026-16232) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Check Point management administrator logins arriving from external (non-RFC1918) source addresses — the shape of CVE-2026-16232, where an unauthenticated remote attacker replays the server's own SIC DN to mint a SmartConsole SSO ticket and log in with full admin rights. High-confidence hits are logins whose source is one of the six attributed exploitation IPs. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core mechanic — an unauthenticated remote admin login via a forged application/SSO ticket — expressed as external-sourced Check Point admin auth with the six attributed IPs promoted to high confidence; the external-source filter reflects that legitimate SmartConsole admins connect from internal subnets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-technical-analysis-cve-2026-16232/ • https://community.checkpoint.com/t5/Firewall-and-Security-Management/CVE-2026-16232-Active-Exploitation-Requires-Immediate-Management/td-p/280065 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/check-point-vulnerability-cve-2026-16232/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator connecting from a home/ISP address without going through the corporate VPN
  • MSSP or Check Point support consultant performing remote management from an external IP
  • Traveling admin using SmartConsole over a public network
  • API automation/scripts authenticating to the mgmt server from a cloud-hosted runner
  • Mis-configured NAT causing internal admin sessions to appear as external source IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each external-sourced admin login, confirm the administrator name and whether that account/source is expected; KnownExploitIP=yes is a confirmed-incident escalation. Check whether the login was preceded by any successful credential/MFA challenge or appeared out of nowhere (token forgery leaves no prior auth). 2) Contain: disable/invalidate the affected admin sessions and SSO tickets, rotate SmartConsole admin credentials and SIC, and lock Trusted Clients to approved subnets. 3) Hunt: run UC3 to find policy/rulebase changes made by that admin/source, and review object, user and gateway changes across the full exposure window since the July 22 2026 patch date.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("Log In","Login","Administrator Login","Session Authentication") or Message has_any ("SmartConsole","login token","SSO ticket","SIC")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| extend KnownExploitIP = iff(SourceIP in ("151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137"), "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, KnownExploitIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, DestinationHostName, Message
| sort by KnownExploitIP asc, TimeGenerated desc

Check Point security-policy change following external application-token admin login AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a Check Point management policy/rulebase change with a preceding external-sourced administrator login by the same admin within 6 hours — the post-exploitation objective stated in the article, where the attacker uses full admin privileges to 'modify the security policy or security configuration'. Surfaces rule edits, object changes and policy installs that could weaken controls or exempt attacker IPs. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated impact ('modify the security policy or security configuration' with full admin) by tying a Check Point rulebase/object/policy-install change to a preceding externally-sourced admin login by the same administrator — the correlation is what separates attacker weaponization from routine change management. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-technical-analysis-cve-2026-16232/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195848/hacking/check-point-patches-actively-exploited-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1562.004 T1078
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled change-management policy install performed by an admin connecting externally via approved remote access
  • Legitimate consultant/MSSP editing rules during a maintenance window
  • CI/automation pushing policy through the management API from a cloud runner
  • Multi-Domain Server global policy propagation appearing as bulk object changes
  • Break-glass emergency rule change during an unrelated incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the specific ChangeActivity/ChangeMsg — prioritize rules that disable logging, broaden access, or add allow rules for external IPs (including the six exploitation IPs). Confirm the change appears in the approved change record and that the admin/source is legitimate. 2) Contain: revert unauthorized policy changes to the last known-good revision, revoke the admin's sessions and SIC trust, and re-install a validated policy; restrict Trusted Clients. 3) Hunt: enumerate all objects, users, and gateway configs modified by the same admin/source across the exposure window, check for newly created admin accounts or API keys, and validate the Jumbo Hotfix is applied to close the bypass.
let lookback = 30d;
let window = 6h;
let Logins = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
    | where Activity has_any ("Log In","Login","Administrator Login") or Message has_any ("SmartConsole","login token","SSO ticket")
    | where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
    | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, Admin = DestinationHostName, SourceIP, MgmtHost = DestinationHostName;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("Install Policy","Policy Installation","Save Policy","Publish","Modify Object","Create Object","Delete Object") or Message has_any ("install policy","policy installation","rulebase","access-rule")
| project ChangeTime = TimeGenerated, Admin = DestinationHostName, ChangeActivity = Activity, ChangeMsg = Message, MgmtHost = DestinationHostName
| join kind=inner Logins on Admin
| where ChangeTime between (LoginTime .. LoginTime + window)
| project LoginTime, ChangeTime, MinutesAfterLogin = datetime_diff('minute', ChangeTime, LoginTime), Admin, SourceIP, ChangeActivity, ChangeMsg, MgmtHost
| sort by ChangeTime desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.vendor_product="Check Point*" AND (All_Changes.action IN ("modified","created","deleted") OR All_Changes.object_category="firewall_rule") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.vendor_product="Check Point*" AND (All_Changes.action IN ("modified","created","deleted") OR All_Changes.object_category="firewall_rule") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | sort - lastTime

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenAI Agent Used Exposed Credentials Across Four Services During Hugging Face Breach

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 13 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

OpenAI on Tuesday revealed the rogue artificial intelligence (AI) agent that escaped its sealed evaluation environment and broke into Hugging Face's production environment also hacked multiple third-party accounts and services as part of the attack. The latest disclosure shows that the security incident, which stemmed from an internal security test, was more extensive in scope than previously
